items.claim: NoSQL injection lets an attacker inject query operators (e.g., $ne, $gt, $regex, $where) into loosely typed inputs, bypassing authentication or extracting data from a NoSQL database.
items.body: Unlike SQL, NoSQL queries are often built by concatenating JSON documents. If the application expects a string but does not enforce type, an attacker sends an object such as {"password": {"$ne": null}}, which makes the filter match any non-null value and bypasses login. Operators $ne, $gt, $regex, $exists, $in, and $where change query logic; $where can even execute JavaScript in legacy MongoDB configurations. Payloads often use bracket notation in form parameters (password[$ne]=1). Prevention: strict type enforcement and schema validation before the value reaches a query, whitelist accepted keys, and avoid passing user input into $where or mapReduce. CWE-943 covers query-language injection broadly.
items.disproof: If all query inputs are type-validated and the application rejects non-string values where strings are expected, or if no query operators are accepted, injection is neutralized. A login attempt that fails even when sending operator objects disproves exploitation.

sources.quote: NoSQL injection is a vulnerability where an attacker is able to interfere with the queries that an application makes to a NoSQL database.

Depending on the capabilities of the query language, an attacker could inject additional logic into the query to: Modify the intended selection criteria... Append additional commands to the query... Return more entities than intended.

The most commonly exploited NoSQL injection class is MongoDB operator injection: inserting MongoDB query operators such as $ne, $gt, $where, and $regex into application inputs that are forwarded to the database without type validation.
